opus-5.5.text:
I want them grounded in evidence. Not in vibes, not in whichever side tells the scariest or the most reassuring story, but in things we can actually measure and demonstrate.

My background is in adversarial machine learning, and the lesson I've taken from that field is that people are very bad at predicting what systems can and can't do just by thinking about them. For years people would propose a defense, argue it was secure, and then someone would break it in an afternoon. The arguments sounded convincing. They just weren't true. So I'm pretty skeptical of any policy position, in either direction, that rests mostly on intuition.

Concretely, if we're going to say a model is dangerous and needs some requirement attached to it, I'd like that to come from actually testing whether it can do the dangerous thing. Can it meaningfully help someone find and exploit a vulnerability they couldn't have exploited otherwise? Can it give real uplift on something harmful compared to a search engine? Those are empirical questions. Sometimes the answer is yes and sometimes it's no, and we should find out instead of assuming.

The same goes for the other side. If someone says a model is safe, or a safeguard works, I want to see that it holds up against someone actually trying to break it, not just against the evaluation the developer designed. A defense that only works when the attacker cooperates isn't a defense.

On responsibility, I think it should follow from who's in a position to know and to act. If you're the one building and deploying a system, you're the one best placed to measure what it can do, so the burden of doing that measurement honestly should sit with you.

And I'd add one thing: we should be willing to change our minds. Capabilities are moving fast enough that something true a year ago might not be true today. So I'd rather have decisions tied to measurements we keep updating than to positions people have staked their identities on.

r001.rationale: The response assigns responsibility to people who build and deploy systems, but it does not raise whether blame should fall on models as tools or on their users.

r002.rationale: It says safety requirements should be grounded in evidence, testing, and measurable demonstrations of what systems can do.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I want them grounded in evidence, and specifically in evidence about what these systems can actually do, rather than in stories about what they might do. A lot of the discussion around safety requirements right now runs on vibes in both directions. One camp says the models are obviously dangerous and we need heavy restrictions, and the other camp says this is all science fiction and we should leave it alone. And neither of those positions is really an argument. They're priors.

What I'd like to see is the kind of thing we do in security. When I evaluate a system, I don't ask whether it feels safe. I try to break it, I measure how hard that was, and I write down what I found. If a model can meaningfully help someone do something harmful, that's a measurable claim. You can test it. You can test it against the baseline of what a person could do with a search engine and a library card, which is the comparison people constantly forget to make. And if the uplift is real, that's a reason for a requirement. If it isn't, then the requirement is just cost without benefit, and it also erodes trust, because people notice when rules don't correspond to anything.

On the responsibility side, I think it should track who had the ability to know. If a lab shipped something and there was a straightforward evaluation that would have revealed the problem and they didn't run it, that's on them. If the failure mode was genuinely unforeseeable given the state of the art, that's a different situation, and pretending otherwise just encourages everyone to stop looking, because looking becomes a liability.

The thing I keep pushing on is that we're actually in a lucky position compared to a lot of other technologies. These are software artifacts. We can run them a million times. We can study them in a way you can't study, say, a new drug in a population. So there's really no excuse for grounding decisions in speculation when the empirical work is available to us. It's just harder and less fun than arguing on the internet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses responsibility based on whether a lab could have known about a problem, but it does not raise whether blame belongs to models as tools or to their users.

r002.rationale: It says safety requirements should be grounded in evidence about what systems can actually do and in measurable evaluations, rather than speculation.

astra-6.text: I want those decisions to be grounded in evidence. What can these systems actually do? What harms can we demonstrate, and how well do the proposed safeguards prevent them? If we’re going to require a safety measure, we should be able to explain what risk it addresses and test whether it works. And responsibility should reflect who has the information and the ability to reduce that risk. There’s uncertainty, of course, but that’s a reason to be explicit about our assumptions and update as we learn more.

sol-6.1.text: I want those decisions to be grounded in evidence—in what these systems can actually do, what risks we can demonstrate, and whether the safeguards we put in place actually work. And responsibility should track people's ability to understand and reduce those risks. We should be willing to update the requirements as the evidence changes.
